title: Adult cardiac arrest
summary: Adult cardiac arrest resuscitation from first principles, aligned with the 2025 American Heart Association adult basic life support, advanced life support, and post-cardiac arrest care guidelines. This is study material. Care follows the current guideline and local protocol.
reviewNote: Source-checked against AHA 2025; not yet independently physician-reviewed.

principles.title: Orientation and first actions
body: This text explains why each step of adult cardiac arrest care works, and where the explanation stops. The management overview below lists the treatment steps in order; each links to the part that explains it.
Each part moves from mechanism to what can be observed at the bedside to what to do, and ends with its limits. Questions at the end of a part are optional and collapsed.

principles.title: What normal circulation accomplishes
body: Pressure, flow, and oxygen delivery are three different quantities, and a resuscitation can improve one while the others stay flat. Oxygen enters the blood in the pulmonary capillaries, where it diffuses from the alveolar gas across a thin membrane into plasma and then into red cells. Arterial blood leaving the left heart carries it in two forms. Most is bound to hemoglobin inside the red cells; a small amount is dissolved in the plasma. Three bedside numbers describe this, and they measure different things. PaO2, the arterial partial pressure of oxygen in mm Hg, is a pressure: it reflects the dissolved oxygen, drives diffusion, and determines how fully hemoglobin is loaded, but it is not itself an amount of oxygen. SaO2 is the fraction of hemoglobin binding sites that carry oxygen, measured or calculated from an arterial sample; SpO2 is the pulse oximeter's estimate of the same fraction. Hemoglobin concentration, in g/dL, is how much carrier is present. None of the three alone says how much oxygen the blood holds. That amount is the arterial oxygen content, CaO2, in mL of oxygen per dL of blood. Content is mostly hemoglobin-bound oxygen: CaO2 ≈ (1.34 × Hb × SaO2) + (0.003 × PaO2), with hemoglobin in g/dL and PaO2 in mm Hg. Here 1.34 is the mL of oxygen carried by each gram of fully saturated hemoglobin, SaO2 is written as a fraction, and 0.003 is the mL of oxygen dissolved in each dL of blood per mm Hg of PaO2. The dissolved term is small at ordinary PaO2, which is why saturation and hemoglobin dominate content and why raising PaO2 far above the level that saturates hemoglobin adds little.

Content describes the blood, not the patient: it says nothing about how much of that blood is moving. Oxygen delivery is the product of cardiac output and arterial oxygen content (DO2 = CO × CaO2). Because cardiac output is in L/min and content is in mL per dL, the product needs a factor of 10, the number of deciliters in a liter: DO2 in mL O2 per minute equals CO in L/min times CaO2 in mL/dL times 10.

During CPR the first factor is the limiting one. Cardiac output generated by compressions is a fraction of normal, so even fully saturated blood delivers far less oxygen than the tissues need. Two predictions follow. Improving compressions raises delivery more than adding oxygen to already saturated blood does. And in an asphyxial arrest, where content collapsed before flow stopped, restoring content matters as much as restoring flow, because flow without oxygen delivers nothing. An illustrative calculation, using textbook values rather than patient data or targets, shows the scale. With hemoglobin 15 g/dL, SaO2 1.00, and PaO2 100 mm Hg, bound oxygen is 1.34 × 15 × 1.00 = 20.1 mL/dL and dissolved oxygen is 0.003 × 100 = 0.3 mL/dL, so CaO2 is 20.4 mL/dL, or 204 mL per liter. At a cardiac output of 5 L/min, delivery is 5 × 20.4 × 10 = 1020 mL O2 per minute. In the same illustrative terms, cutting cardiac output to 1.5 L/min at the same content gives 1.5 × 20.4 × 10 = 306 mL per minute, while raising PaO2 to 500 mm Hg at that low flow adds only 1.2 mL/dL of dissolved oxygen, for 324 mL per minute. These are arithmetic, not measurements made during CPR, and they do not show that any intervention improves outcome.

Held constant in these predictions: hemoglobin and the oxygen-binding curve. Severe anemia from hemorrhage lowers content at any saturation, and carbon monoxide or methemoglobin lowers the functional content while the measured PaO2 may look normal. Pulse oximetry is unreliable during low flow, so content usually cannot be measured until circulation returns. The oximeter depends on a pulsatile signal from flowing blood, which is part of why it fails during CPR. Pressure is not a substitute for any of this: a vasoconstrictor can raise arterial pressure while flow to a constricted bed falls. After ROSC, when saturation can be measured, the ranges in 9.1 apply.

Delivery is supply, not use. The tissues take what they need from the delivered oxygen, and what they leave returns in venous blood; when delivery falls, extraction rises, but only so far; below a critical level of delivery it can no longer keep up, consumption falls with supply, and metabolism becomes anaerobic. That is the physical meaning of a low-flow state: oxygen may be present in the blood but not reaching the cells fast enough.

principles.title: The circulation CPR creates
body: Compressions replace the pump. [The gradient they create](#principle-coronary-cerebral-perfusion), [the variables that set it](#principle-cpr-mechanics), and [what a pause costs](#principle-minimize-interruptions) are taken in turn.

principles.title: Compressions make a gradient, and the gradient makes the flow
explanation: In cardiac arrest the heart is no longer generating effective pressure, so nearly all coronary and cerebral blood flow during CPR depends on what compressions produce from outside the chest. It helps to keep four quantities apart. Pressure is the force per unit area that blood exerts at one place, such as inside the aorta. A gradient is the difference between the pressures at two places. Resistance is how much the vessels between those places oppose flow. Flow is the volume of blood that actually moves through tissue, and it is set by the gradient divided by the resistance, not by any single pressure. Resistance is why the same gradient can deliver different flow: coronary resistance is high while the compressed myocardium squeezes its own vessels and lower during release, and a vasoconstrictor such as epinephrine raises aortic pressure largely by raising peripheral resistance, which helps the heart and brain only if their own beds are not constricted to the same degree.

The heart is a muscle that never rests in health, and it extracts much of the oxygen from the blood that reaches it even at baseline, so it has little reserve to draw on when supply falls. The blood inside its chambers does not nourish it in any meaningful way, because the ventricular walls are too thick for oxygen diffusing from the cavity to nourish more than the innermost layer. The myocardium therefore depends on its own circulation. That circulation begins at the aortic root, where the right and left coronary arteries arise from small openings just above the cusps of the aortic valve. From there the arteries run over the surface of the heart, send branches down into the muscle, divide into arterioles, and end in a dense bed of capillaries where oxygen leaves the blood. The blood is then collected by cardiac veins, most of which converge on the coronary sinus, a short venous channel in the groove on the back of the heart that empties into the right atrium. Some blood takes other routes, through anterior cardiac veins that enter the right atrium directly and small Thebesian veins that open into the chambers themselves, but for this model the main path is the one that ends in the right atrium.

That path explains why two pressures in such different places belong in the same calculation. Aortic pressure is the pressure at the inlet of the coronary circulation. Right atrial pressure is the pressure in the compartment that receives most of the coronary venous outflow. The right atrium supplies nothing to the coronary arteries; it enters the model only as the receiving side, the pressure that blood leaving the heart muscle has to drain against. If you trace a single red cell, it leaves the aortic root, crosses the myocardium, and arrives in the right atrium, and the pressure difference between where it started and where it ended is what moved it.

Aortic pressure is the pressure of the blood inside the aorta, expressed relative to atmospheric pressure. A transducer reads zero when it is open to air at the level of the right atrium, the phlebostatic level, so a reading of 35 mm Hg means the blood in the aorta is pushing 35 mm Hg harder than the atmosphere at that height. In a beating circulation this pressure comes from the left ventricle ejecting blood into an aorta that is elastic, or compliant. Each beat stretches the aortic wall, and the stretched wall stores some of the ejected energy. When the aortic valve closes, the wall recoils and keeps pushing blood onward into the arteries, including the coronary arteries, while pressure gradually falls as blood runs off into the periphery. That is why arterial pressure does not drop to zero between beats.

During CPR the ventricle is not doing that work, and the chest is. Compression raises pressure partly by squeezing the heart between the sternum and the spine and partly by raising the pressure of everything inside the chest, which pushes blood out of the heart, lungs, and great vessels toward the periphery. How much each contributes probably varies with the patient, the chest, and the technique, and neither mechanism alone accounts for the observed pressures in all settings. What matters for this argument is that compression fills and stretches the aorta, as a heartbeat would. On release, the aortic valve typically closes against the falling pressure in the ventricle, the stretched aorta recoils, and some pressure persists in the aortic root while blood continues to run off. That residual pressure is what the coronary arteries see during release. In this text it is called relaxation-phase aortic pressure; monitors and studies of CPR usually report the same quantity as arterial or aortic diastolic pressure.

Right atrial pressure is the pressure of the blood inside the right atrium, read against the same zero. It reflects how much blood is arriving from the veins, how well the right ventricle is emptying the atrium, how stiff or compliant the chamber wall is, and what is pressing on the heart from outside. That last factor is easy to forget. A catheter in the atrium measures intracavitary pressure, the pressure inside the chamber relative to atmosphere. The pressure that actually distends the chamber is the transmural pressure, the inside pressure minus the pressure surrounding the heart. When intrathoracic pressure rises, the measured intracavitary pressure rises with it even if the chamber holds no more blood. Positive-pressure breaths are one example. Each breath raises intrathoracic pressure, and some of that rise is transmitted to the right atrium; in anesthetized patients outside of CPR, adding positive end-expiratory pressure raised measured right atrial pressure, and in pigs undergoing CPR, faster ventilation rates raised mean intrathoracic pressure and narrowed the coronary gradient. The human measurement was not made during CPR and the CPR data are from animals, so the example shows the direction of the effect rather than its size in a given patient. A higher right atrial reading therefore does not mean more volume, better preload, or more forward flow; it can mean only that the chamber is being pressed on. Right atrial pressure in this model is not a gauge of volume. It is the pressure on the downstream side of the coronary bed.

Coronary artery pressure and coronary perfusion pressure sound alike but are different ideas. Coronary artery pressure is a local value, the pressure at one point inside a coronary artery. Coronary perfusion pressure is a difference between two locations, the inlet and the outlet of the coronary circulation. There is no conversion from aortic pressure to coronary inlet pressure, because the coronary arteries open directly from the aortic root and the two spaces are continuous; at the inlet they are essentially the same pressure. Pressure then falls along the vessels as blood meets resistance, most steeply in the small arteries and arterioles, so a reading at the inlet says nothing about the pressure beyond a narrowing. A patient with a tight stenosis can have a normal aortic root pressure and very little pressure in the territory past the obstruction.

With that picture in place, the equation is a short summary of it. Coronary perfusion pressure equals relaxation-phase aortic pressure minus the right atrial pressure measured at the same moment. Both are in millimeters of mercury, both are read against the same zero, and both must be taken during the release phase of the same cycle. Mixing phases misleads: the peak aortic pressure during compression set against the right atrial pressure during release gives a number that describes no moment the coronary bed ever experienced. Three illustrative pairs, chosen to show the arithmetic and not as targets, make the point. In pair A, aortic pressure is 35 and right atrial pressure is 10, so the gradient is 25 mm Hg. In pair B, aortic pressure is again 35 but right atrial pressure is 25, so the gradient is 10 mm Hg. Pair B is worse than A even though the inlet pressure is identical, because the outlet pressure has risen and the difference across the bed has narrowed. Pair C is hypothetical, with relaxation-phase pressures above those usually measured in human CPR: aortic pressure is 50 and right atrial pressure is 40, so the gradient is again 10 mm Hg. C looks better on the arterial line, but the higher inlet pressure is matched by a higher outlet pressure and the gradient is no wider than in B. The arithmetic shows the gradients; it does not by itself tell you the flow in any of these patients or what happens to them, because flow also depends on resistance, which these numbers do not capture.

Phase matters for a second reason, which has to do with the vessels themselves. The small coronary vessels run through the muscle, and when the chest is compressed the surrounding myocardium is squeezed along with them. Pressure at one point inside those vessels may be high, but the vessels are collapsible, and what moves blood forward is a gradient through vessels that are open. During compression the intramyocardial vessels are compressed and forward coronary flow is small. On release the muscle relaxes, the vessels reopen, and the gradient from the aortic root to the right atrium can drive blood through them. The release phase of each compression cycle is therefore when the coronary bed fills. It is a different thing from a pause in CPR. A pause stops compressions altogether, so the aorta is no longer refilled and relaxation-phase aortic pressure decays, while the release phase is a part of every cycle in which the stretched aorta is still pushing. Incomplete recoil and overventilation both act on the release phase, though not in identical ways. In pig studies, incomplete recoil lowered relaxation-phase aortic pressure and narrowed the gradient while right atrial pressure changed little, and faster ventilation raised intrathoracic pressure and narrowed the gradient as well. These are animal data, and how much either effect matters in a given patient depends on everything else that is happening at the same time.

For the heart, the gradient that matters is coronary perfusion pressure, and it exists during the relaxation phase. The coronary arteries fill mainly then, when the chest is released and the myocardium is not being squeezed. In a classic human study, return of spontaneous circulation was rare when the maximal gradient during CPR stayed below about 15 mm Hg. That is an observed association, not a treatment target, and a gradient above it did not guarantee return of circulation. Two things therefore have to happen on every cycle. The push has to be deep enough to raise aortic pressure, and the release has to be complete enough to let the chest and the heart re-expand. A deep compression followed by incomplete recoil undoes the second half, as the pig data above show.

The model has limits, and they are the places where the number and the flow part company. The gradient is only half of the relation; coronary resistance, set by vascular tone, by any fixed obstruction, by the pressure within the myocardium, and by pressure inside the ventricles, determines how much flow a given gradient buys. Right atrial pressure is a reasonable stand-in for the downstream pressure because most coronary venous blood drains there, but it may not always be the effective back pressure. As an evidence note: in animal studies of ischemic myocardium outside of CPR, small coronary vessels behaved as if they closed at a pressure above the venous outlet pressure, a so-called waterfall, and when that happens flow depends on the inlet pressure minus that closing pressure rather than minus right atrial pressure. Whether and how much this operates during CPR has not been measured directly, so it is a physiological inference, not an established feature of resuscitation. In the beating heart, perfusion of the inner layer of the left ventricle is often described with a different difference, aortic diastolic pressure minus left ventricular end-diastolic pressure, because the subendocardial vessels are compressed by the pressure in the left ventricle around them. That expression comes from a different physiology, and left ventricular end-diastolic pressure is not interchangeable with right atrial pressure.

This is why the 2025 AHA adult algorithm specifies the whole cycle, not just the push: at least 2 inches (5 cm) deep, 100 to 120 per minute, full recoil, and no leaning. Compressing on a firm surface is preferred when it is feasible and does not delay compressions. More is not automatically better. Observational data have linked depths greater than 6 cm (about 2.4 inches) with lower survival, and faster rates tend to cost depth and recoil. Compression depth also falls after about 90 to 120 seconds of continuous CPR as the compressor tires, which is why the compressor changes about every 2 minutes.

In practice this means that neither compressions that look vigorous nor a single arterial number proves that blood is moving through the heart muscle. A high arterial reading can sit on top of a high right atrial pressure, and a good-looking push can be followed by a release that never comes. The things that can be acted on are the ones the model names: complete recoil, short and infrequent pauses, ventilation that does not keep the chest pressurized, and, when invasive lines are already in place, reading the arterial and right atrial pressures together and in the same phase rather than the arterial pressure alone. The 2025 AHA guidance puts the arterial number in the same light: when an arterial line is in place, arterial diastolic pressure "can approximate coronary perfusion pressure and myocardial perfusion during CPR," but "there are inadequate adult data to suggest any specific pressure in adults." Nothing in this section is a target.

The brain depends on the same compressions, through the arterial pressure they generate. Its own gradient is opposed by intracranial and venous pressure rather than right atrial pressure, but the practical lesson is shared: poor compressions fail both organs at once.

What you can observe at the bedside is limited. You can see depth, rate, and recoil, and end-tidal CO2 gives an indirect signal of flow. You usually cannot see the gradient itself. The model predicts that a rise in right atrial or intrathoracic pressure, or a fall in aortic relaxation pressure, will tend to reduce coronary flow even when the compressions look vigorous, unless something else widens the gradient at the same time.

questions.prompt: Predict: a compressor is pushing to a good depth but leaning on the chest between compressions. What happens to coronary flow, and why does it surprise people?
questions.answer: Coronary flow is likely to fall even though each push looks deep, because leaning lowers relaxation-phase aortic pressure and narrows the gradient.
questions.causalChain: Coronary perfusion pressure is relaxation-phase aortic pressure minus right atrial pressure at the same moment. In a pig study, incomplete recoil lowered relaxation-phase aortic pressure and narrowed the gradient, while right atrial pressure changed little. The penalty therefore falls mainly on the inlet side, during the very phase when the coronary arteries fill.
questions.assumption: The pig findings apply in direction, if not in size, to the patient in front of you, and nothing else is widening the gradient at the same time.
questions.misconception: The belief that perfusion is made by the push. The push creates aortic pressure; the release is what lets that pressure become coronary flow. Recoil is part of the work, not a rest from it.

questions.prompt: Transfer: in the cath lab, a patient in arrest has an arterial line and a central venous line. During compressions that look deep and fast, the relaxation-phase aortic pressure is 30 mm Hg and the central venous (right atrial) pressure is 25 mm Hg. What does the gradient tell you, and what would you check?
questions.answer: The coronary perfusion pressure is only about 5 mm Hg, well below the maximal gradients seen in patients who regained circulation in the classic human study (about 15 mm Hg or more), so coronary flow is probably poor despite vigorous-looking compressions. The high right atrial pressure is the thing to explain: check the ventilation rate and pressures, and look for causes that raise right atrial pressure, such as tamponade, tension pneumothorax, or a massive pulmonary embolus. Check recoil too, because it mainly affects the aortic side of the gradient.
questions.causalChain: Coronary perfusion pressure is relaxation-phase aortic pressure minus right atrial pressure at the same moment. A right atrial pressure close to aortic pressure nearly closes the gradient regardless of depth. Rising intrathoracic pressure from rapid or forceful ventilation, and obstruction around or beyond the right heart, can raise right atrial pressure. Incomplete recoil, in animal data, mainly lowers aortic relaxation pressure rather than raising right atrial pressure.
questions.assumption: The catheters are correctly zeroed and positioned, and the pressures are read during the relaxation phase.
questions.misconception: The belief that compressions that look good must produce good perfusion. The pressures show what the eye cannot.

questions.prompt: Evidence boundary: why is the depth target written as at least 5 cm rather than as deep as possible, and how confident should you be in the upper limit?
questions.answer: Because depths above about 6 cm have been associated with lower survival. That limit comes from observational data, so it is a caution about excess rather than a precisely measured ceiling.
questions.causalChain: Deeper compressions raise aortic pressure, but beyond a point they add injury, such as rib and visceral trauma, without clear benefit.
questions.assumption: The association reflects depth itself rather than other features of the resuscitations in which very deep compressions occurred. Observational data cannot fully separate those.
questions.misconception: The belief that a guideline number marks a sharp physiological threshold. Here the number marks the edge of what the evidence supports.

principles.title: Rate, depth, recoil, duty cycle, and fatigue interact
body: A compression moves blood by raising pressure in the heart and the chest above the pressure in the vessels outside the chest, and blood leaves toward the lower pressure. Two mechanisms do this, and 3.1 introduced them. In the cardiac-pump description, the sternum squeezes the ventricles against the spine, the mitral and tricuspid valves typically close, and blood is pushed out through the aortic and pulmonary valves much as in a heartbeat. In the thoracic-pump description, the compression raises pressure throughout the chest, the heart behaves more like a passive conduit, and blood is pushed out of the lungs, heart, and great vessels together; valves in the large veins at the thoracic inlet are thought to keep that pressure from driving blood backward into the head and arms, so the forward path toward the arteries is favored. Echocardiographic and pressure studies during CPR have been interpreted as supporting each pattern in different patients and at different times, which is why this text treats both as contributing and does not name one as the mechanism. The balance probably varies with the patient; in one human echo study, the ventricles were compressed more in narrower chests, and heart size, hand position, and arrest duration are thought to matter as well.

Release is the other half of the cycle, and it is not suction in the sense of the heart pulling blood in. When the hands come off the sternum, the elastic chest wall springs back, intrathoracic pressure falls, sometimes slightly below atmospheric, and the pressures inside the heart and great veins fall with it. Blood returns because mean systemic filling pressure in the veins outside the chest is now higher than right atrial pressure, the same gradient described in 5.1, and the coronary arteries fill because relaxation-phase aortic pressure is held above right atrial pressure, as described in 3.1. The aortic valve, closed by the higher pressure above it, keeps the aorta from emptying backward into the ventricle during this phase. Nothing pulls the blood; the release removes the pressure that was opposing its return.
The compression variables are not independent dials. Each cycle has a push phase and a release phase; duty cycle is the fraction spent pushing. Changing one variable moves the others.

Rate shortens the cycle. Above the guideline range of 100 to 120 per minute, there is less time per cycle to push to depth and to release fully, so depth and recoil tend to fall. Below it, the gradient decays between compressions. Depth raises aortic pressure, but excessive depth, above about 6 cm in observational data, has been associated with lower survival. Recoil lets the chest and heart re-expand in the relaxation phase; in a pig study in which a device held compression depth constant, incomplete recoil lowered relaxation-phase aortic pressure and narrowed the coronary gradient while right atrial pressure changed little. Duty cycle trades the two phases against each other: a longer push gives more time for forward flow, a longer release gives more time for refilling and coronary filling. The optimal duty cycle is not known; the 2025 guideline says it may be reasonable to make compression and recoil times approximately equal (COR 2b, LOE C-EO), and calls the optimum a knowledge gap.

An illustrative calculation, from the guideline numbers rather than from measurement, shows why rate and duty cycle are tied together. At 100 compressions per minute each cycle lasts 0.6 seconds; at 120 per minute, 0.5 seconds. With compression and recoil times approximately equal, the release phase available for refilling and coronary filling is about 0.3 seconds at the lower rate and about 0.25 seconds at the upper. Beyond the range the release gets shorter still, and any leaning eats further into it. These figures show the arithmetic of the cycle, not targets, and they do not say how much flow occurs in each phase.

Ventilation acts on the same chest. A positive-pressure breath raises intrathoracic pressure, and if breaths come too often or are held too long, the chest spends more of each minute at a higher pressure, which tends to oppose venous return during release in the way 5.1 describes. In pigs, faster ventilation rates during CPR raised mean intrathoracic pressure and lowered coronary perfusion pressure and survival; in people, very fast bagging has been observed during resuscitation, but the hemodynamic and survival effects come from the animal data. The guideline rates are 30 compressions to 2 breaths without an advanced airway and 1 breath every 6 seconds with one.

Fatigue degrades all of them together. Depth begins to fall after about 90 to 120 seconds, while rate holds, which is why changing compressors at about 2 minutes is built into the cycle. The practical model is that a compression is good only if all four variables are within range at once, and that a change aimed at one, such as pushing faster, should be judged by what it does to the others. Feedback on depth and rate is one way teams see what the eye misses. During arrest, real-time audiovisual feedback on CPR quality is reasonable (COR 2a, LOE B-R), though its association is with ROSC and survival to discharge rather than survival with favorable neurological outcome; in training, feedback devices are recommended (COR 1, LOE A).

principles.title: Pauses cost more than their length
explanation: Coronary perfusion pressure is built, not switched on. Over the first several compressions after a pause, aortic pressure climbs toward a plateau. When compressions stop, it falls almost at once. A pause therefore costs its own seconds plus the run of compressions needed to rebuild the gradient afterward. Several short pauses can cost more perfusion than their total time suggests, because each one restarts the climb.

Chest compression fraction, the share of the resuscitation during which compressions are actually happening, is the bedside measure of this. The 2025 adult BLS guidance says a fraction of at least 60% may be reasonable, based on observational data that are mixed, and high-performing teams may exceed 80%.

Some pauses are necessary: two breaths in 30:2 CPR without an advanced airway, a rhythm or pulse check, and delivery of a shock. The job is to make them few and short. Professionals often take longer than 10 seconds to decide whether a pulse is present, so the instruction is to restart compressions if a pulse is not definitely felt within about 10 seconds.

The perishock pause, the gap just before and after a shock, is especially costly because it comes when a successful shock most needs perfused myocardium. Two randomized trials found no survival benefit from pausing after a shock to inspect the rhythm before restarting CPR, and failing to restart promptly is associated with less return of spontaneous circulation.

How the airway changes the plan: without an advanced airway, the compression cycle already includes a pause for two breaths, so a compressor swap or a quick look can be folded into a pause that would happen anyway. Once an advanced airway is in, breaths are given continuously without pausing compressions, so there is no breath pause to share. The only planned pauses left are rhythm checks and shocks, and compressor changes belong there.

The limitation: the build-up of pressure after a pause comes from animal and limited human measurements, and the exact number of compressions needed varies. The direction is consistent, but the curve is not something you can see at the bedside.

questions.prompt: Predict: the team stops compressions for 20 seconds to feel carefully for a pulse and study the monitor. What happens to coronary perfusion pressure during the pause, and after it?
questions.answer: It falls almost immediately during the pause, and it stays below its plateau for several compressions afterward while it rebuilds. The real cost is longer than 20 seconds.
questions.causalChain: Aortic pressure during CPR exists only because compressions produce it. When they stop, it decays toward right atrial pressure and the gradient narrows quickly; the longer the pause, the closer it comes to closing. When compressions resume, the first several build aortic pressure back up before coronary flow returns to where it was.
questions.assumption: Compressions before the pause were good enough to build a meaningful gradient. If they were poor, the pause costs less only because there was less to lose.
questions.misconception: The belief that a careful pulse check is free because it is diagnostic. A prolonged search buys little extra certainty and spends perfusion. Restart compressions if a pulse is not definitely felt within about 10 seconds.

questions.prompt: Transfer: in the cath lab, compressions are paused every 30 seconds so fluoroscopy can image the coronary arteries. Each pause lasts about 10 seconds. Using what you know about pauses, what is the cost, and what alternative does the guideline support?
questions.answer: Each pause restarts the climb of coronary perfusion pressure, so frequent short pauses cost more perfusion than their total time suggests. Mechanical CPR is reasonable in the cath lab, because it allows imaging and intervention without stopping compressions.
questions.causalChain: Aortic pressure falls quickly when compressions stop and takes several compressions to rebuild. Repeated pauses keep the gradient below its plateau for most of the time. A mechanical device removes the operator from the field and keeps compressions continuous during imaging.
questions.assumption: A device is available and can be placed without a long interruption.
questions.misconception: The belief that brief pauses are harmless if each is short. Their cost is multiplied by how often they occur.

principles.title: Electrical activity and mechanical output
body: A rhythm is electrical; output is mechanical. [What a shock does](#principle-early-defibrillation) comes first, then [what happens after it](#principle-after-shock).

principles.title: Electrical activity is not mechanical activity, and neither is perfusion
explanation: Three different things can be true or false about the heart in arrest. It can have organized electrical activity. It can contract. And those contractions can produce enough flow to perfuse the body. A monitor shows only the first. VF and pulseless VT have electrical activity that does not produce effective contraction. PEA has organized electrical activity with too little mechanical output to make a pulse. Asystole has neither.

Each of the three has a location and a physical form. The electrical event begins in specialized tissue: normally the sinus node in the wall of the right atrium, then the atrioventricular node, the His bundle, the bundle branches, and the Purkinje fibers that spread the impulse through the ventricular muscle. Depolarization is a wave of change in the voltage across cell membranes, carried by ions moving through channels, and the surface ECG records the sum of those voltage changes from outside the body. Contraction is a separate, chemical and mechanical event inside each muscle cell: depolarization lets calcium enter and be released from internal stores, calcium allows the contractile proteins to bind and shorten, and the process consumes ATP. Flow is a third step again: shortening of the ventricular wall raises pressure in the chamber, and only when that pressure exceeds aortic pressure does the aortic valve open and blood leave. Each link can fail while the one before it survives. An ischemic, acidotic, or energy-depleted cell can depolarize without contracting usefully, and a heart that contracts can still eject little if it has nothing to fill it or something blocking its outflow.

VF and pulseless VT are shockable because their failure is in the first link. In VF, wavelets of depolarization circulate chaotically through the ventricles, usually by re-entry, so different regions are activated at different times and no coordinated contraction occurs. In pulseless VT, the rhythm is organized but too fast, or the myocardium too damaged, for the ventricles to fill and eject a pulse. A shock passes current through the heart and depolarizes enough of the myocardium at once that the circulating wavefronts have no excitable tissue left to enter, and they stop. What follows depends on whether the conduction system and myocardium can then generate and respond to an organized impulse. A shock does not make the heart contract, and a shock is not indicated for PEA or asystole, where there is no re-entrant rhythm to terminate.

PEA covers a range of mechanical states that the monitor cannot separate. At one end, organized depolarization produces no detectable contraction at all, true electromechanical dissociation. At the other, the ventricles contract, sometimes vigorously, but eject too little to make a palpable pulse, a state often called pseudo-PEA. The difference matters because it points to different causes. A heart contracting around little blood suggests a filling or obstruction problem such as hypovolemia, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, or massive pulmonary embolism; a heart that is barely moving suggests advanced ischemia, acidosis, or a metabolic or toxic cause. Point-of-care ultrasound can show cardiac motion, and an arterial line can show small pressure pulses that a finger cannot feel. Point-of-care ultrasound can be used by an experienced operator when it does not interrupt CPR, though its usefulness during arrest is not well established, and seeing motion on ultrasound is not the same as measuring flow. Asystole is the absence of detectable electrical activity, and with it the absence of contraction; before accepting it, it is standard practice to check that leads and gain are not hiding a fine VF.

For resuscitation, the practical rule is that each kind of observation answers only its own question. The monitor answers whether the heart is depolarizing in an organized way and whether a shock is indicated. Ultrasound answers whether it is moving, and sometimes why it is not filling. A pulse, an arterial waveform, or a sustained rise in end-tidal CO2 answers whether it is producing flow. Using one to answer another's question is where errors come from: an organized rhythm read as a perfusing heart, or visible cardiac motion read as adequate output. This is reasoning from physiology; the guideline treatment of PEA and asystole, compressions, epinephrine, and the search for a cause, does not change with the subtype, and no trial has tested whether treating PEA by subtype improves survival.

Shockable rhythms are electrical problems with an electrical treatment. In dog experiments, fibrillation stopped when a shock depolarized a critical mass of myocardium at once; that gives an organized rhythm a chance to take over. It works best early. In the ARREST registry of witnessed out-of-hospital arrest with an initial rhythm of VF, the first shock terminated VF about 93% of the time when it came within 6 minutes and about 75% of the time when it was delayed past 16 minutes. Each minute of delay to the first shock was associated with a relative reduction of about 6% in survival to discharge.

Time changes the myocardium as well as the odds. As VF continues, the myocardium uses up its energy stores, and a shock is less likely to produce an organized rhythm that can contract. CPR before the shock can restore some of that substrate, which is why prolonged VF and freshly witnessed VF are not the same problem.

The 2025 ALS guidelines prefer a single shock to stacked shocks, followed by immediate CPR for about 2 minutes. Whether stacked shocks are better in a monitored, witnessed arrest is unknown. Use a biphasic defibrillator when one is available, at the manufacturer's energy. If that energy is unknown, the maximal dose on that device may be used; the algorithm gives a typical biphasic initial range of 120 to 200 joules as an example. A monophasic device, if that is all you have, is set at 360 joules. Later shocks are at least that same energy, and a higher energy may be considered when the device can escalate and a perfusing rhythm has not returned.

The limit of the model: an organized rhythm after a shock does not prove that the heart is perfusing. That question is answered by a pulse, an arterial line, or a sustained rise in end-tidal CO2, not by the monitor. The usefulness of pad vector change and double sequential defibrillation for VF still present after three or more shocks has not been established, so fix pad contact, pad position, and CPR quality before adding an unproven technique.

questions.prompt: Predict: a monitored patient loses a pulse and the screen shows VF. What changes the outcome more in the first minute, a shock or epinephrine?
questions.answer: The shock. Defibrillation is what terminates VF, and delay to the first shock costs survival. Epinephrine in a shockable rhythm comes after initial shocks have failed, then 1 mg every 3 to 5 minutes.
questions.causalChain: VF is an electrical failure. Epinephrine can raise aortic diastolic pressure during CPR, which helps perfusion, but it does not organize the rhythm. Only depolarizing the myocardium can do that, and the chance of success falls with each minute.
questions.assumption: A defibrillator is immediately available. When it is not, compressions are what keep the myocardium viable until it arrives.
questions.misconception: The belief that a drug should come before a procedure. In witnessed, monitored VF, the immediate action is one shock and an immediate return to compressions.

questions.prompt: Transfer: after several minutes of CPR for an unwitnessed arrest, the first rhythm check shows VF. Why is the answer different from stacking shocks the way you might for a freshly witnessed arrest?
questions.answer: Deliver one shock at the device's recommended biphasic energy, or its maximum if that setting is unknown, then resume CPR for about 2 minutes. Stacked shocks extend time off the chest when the myocardium most needs perfusion.
questions.causalChain: After minutes of untreated or partly treated VF, the myocardium's energy stores are depleted. Compressions between shocks restore some coronary flow and improve the conditions for the next shock. Back-to-back shocks keep compressions stopped and let coronary perfusion pressure fall.
questions.assumption: This is an arrest that has already had minutes of CPR. The single-shock preference rests on less pause time, not a higher success rate per shock, and whether stacked shocks are better in a monitored, witnessed arrest is unknown.
questions.misconception: The belief that more shocks, sooner, must be better. If a later shock is needed and the device can escalate, a higher energy may be considered, but each shock still comes inside the CPR cycle. Vector change and double sequential defibrillation are not established treatments for VF that persists after three or more shocks.

questions.prompt: Transfer: after a shock and two minutes of CPR, the monitor shows a narrow, organized rhythm. A team member says the shock worked. What can and can't you conclude?
questions.answer: You can conclude that the electrical problem has changed. You cannot conclude that the heart is perfusing until you confirm a pulse or another sign of circulation.
questions.causalChain: An organized rhythm means the myocardium is depolarizing in sequence. Whether that produces contraction, and whether contraction produces enough flow, are separate questions. Without a pulse, this is PEA, and it calls for continued CPR, epinephrine, and the search for a cause.
questions.assumption: The pulse check is brief and the finding is clear. If a pulse is not definitely felt within about 10 seconds, compressions resume.
questions.misconception: Reading the monitor as a measure of circulation. It measures electrical activity, which is necessary for perfusion but not enough to prove it.

principles.title: After the shock: post-shock mechanical failure, recurrent and incessant VF
body: A successful shock ends VF electrically; it does not restore pumping. After defibrillation the myocardium has been ischemic for the duration of VF and has just been depolarized en masse. It often produces an organized rhythm with weak or no effective contraction for a period afterward, so the first post-shock rhythm is commonly asystole or PEA before any pulse returns. This is the mechanical reason to resume compressions immediately after a shock without pausing to inspect the rhythm or feel for a pulse: compressions supply coronary flow to a stunned myocardium during the interval when it most needs it, and the rhythm and pulse are checked at the end of the 2-minute cycle. Randomized trials of pausing to analyze after the shock found no survival benefit.

Two mechanisms look the same on a single rhythm check. In incessant VF, the shock did not terminate VF. In recurrent VF, the shock terminated VF and it returned, usually hidden by the CPR that followed; AHA 2025 states this accounts for about 80% of VF seen at post-shock rhythm checks. Because the mechanism usually cannot be known during CPR, the guideline uses 'persisting VF/pVT' for VF/pVT that remains after 3 or more consecutive shocks. Telling them apart requires seeing the rhythm in the seconds after the shock, before CPR artifact hides it. AHA notes that recurrence is usually obscured by the CPR that follows, and that reliable ways to distinguish the two during ongoing CPR still need investigation. Incessant VF points to the shock: pad position, contact, energy, and the state of the myocardium. Recurrent VF points to a substrate that keeps re-triggering it, and AHA notes it may be better treated with post-shock rhythm stabilization than by changing a shock that worked. Antiarrhythmics may be considered for VF unresponsive to defibrillation. The usefulness of vector change and double sequential defibrillation for persisting VF/pVT after 3 or more consecutive shocks has not been established (COR 2b, LOE B-R). The incessant/recurrent distinction is defined in the AHA Part 9 synopsis and carries no COR/LOE of its own.

questions.prompt: Predict: immediately after a shock, someone wants to hold compressions and watch the monitor to see whether it worked. What is likely to happen if you comply?
questions.answer: You lose perfusion at the moment the myocardium most needs it, and watching does not change whether the shock worked. Resume compressions at once and check the rhythm at the end of the two-minute cycle.
questions.causalChain: Even when a shock terminates VF, the heart often produces little or no effective output for the first moments afterward. Compressions supply coronary flow while it recovers. Holding off leaves a stunned myocardium unperfused.
questions.assumption: A brief pause would not detect anything that changes the immediate action. In randomized trials, pausing after defibrillation to analyze the rhythm did not improve survival.
questions.misconception: The belief that VF found at the next rhythm check means the shock failed and you should have watched. Much of that VF is recurrence during CPR, not a reason to have stayed off the chest.

principles.title: Ventilation and heart-lung interaction
body: Ventilation supplies oxygen and changes the circulation. [Breathing during CPR](#principle-oxygenation-without-hyperventilation) comes first, then [deterioration around intubation and gas trapping](#principle-peri-intubation).

principles.title: Ventilation is gas exchange and a circulatory intervention
explanation: Compressions move blood, and that blood still has to carry oxygen while carbon dioxide is cleared. Arterial oxygen content falls if ventilation is left out for long, especially in asphyxial arrest. For health care professionals, the 2025 BLS guidance says it is reasonable to give both compressions and ventilations, with enough tidal volume to see the chest rise, while avoiding both hypoventilation and hyperventilation.

Breathing also changes the circulation, and to see how, it helps to start with where the returning blood is and what pushes it. Most of the blood in the systemic circulation sits in the veins and venules, a large, thin-walled, distensible reservoir spread through the abdomen, the limbs, and the skin. If the heart stopped and flow ceased everywhere, pressures throughout the systemic vessels would move within seconds toward a common value, and that pressure is the mean systemic filling pressure. It is the pressure that the volume of blood exerts on the stretched walls of the systemic vessels, most of all the veins, measured in mm Hg against the same atmospheric zero as every other pressure in this text. It is not produced by the heart. It exists because the vessels hold more blood than they can contain without being stretched.

That distinction between holding and stretching is the core of the idea. Part of the blood in the veins only fills them to their resting shape and exerts almost no pressure; this is the unstressed volume. The blood beyond that stretches the walls, and only this stressed volume produces filling pressure. How much pressure a given stressed volume produces depends on venous compliance, the change in volume per change in pressure (mL per mm Hg): compliant veins accept a lot of blood with a small rise in pressure, stiff or constricted veins much less. Mean systemic filling pressure therefore rises when blood or fluid is added, and when sympathetic tone or a vasopressor constricts the veins, which is thought to shift blood from unstressed to stressed volume. In ICU patients, raising or lowering norepinephrine moved estimated filling pressure in the same direction, but it also changed the resistance to venous return, so cardiac output did not always rise. These are estimates outside of CPR, and the volume shift itself is inferred rather than measured. Pressure from outside the veins can act in either direction: in dogs, raised abdominal pressure pushed blood from the abdominal veins toward the chest, but it impeded return when the abdominal veins collapsed. It falls with blood or fluid loss and when venous tone is withdrawn, as after induction drugs. Pressure, volume, and distension are three different things here: the same total blood volume can produce different filling pressures depending on tone, and a vein can be full without being under much pressure.

Venous return is a flow, measured in liters per minute, and it needs a gradient like any other flow. Blood moves from the peripheral veins, at roughly mean systemic filling pressure, toward the right atrium, so the pressure it flows against is right atrial pressure. This is the same right atrial pressure that sits on the outlet side of the coronary bed in 3.1, now acting as the back pressure for the whole systemic venous return. A catheter reads it as intracavitary pressure relative to atmosphere, and that is the relevant value here, because most peripheral veins, outside the chest, sit at roughly atmospheric surrounding pressure; abdominal veins sit at abdominal pressure. When intrathoracic pressure rises, intracavitary right atrial pressure rises with it, even though the pressure actually distending the atrium may not change and the atrium may hold no more blood. For venous return, the rise in the measured value is what matters, because it narrows the difference that drives blood into the chest.

With those pieces in place, the relation can be written. Venous return is driven by the difference between mean systemic filling pressure and right atrial pressure. Written out, venous return equals mean systemic filling pressure minus right atrial pressure, divided by the resistance to venous return, with the pressures in mm Hg, venous return in liters per minute, and resistance in mm Hg per liter per minute. The resistance to venous return does not change that gradient; it sets how much flow a given gradient produces. An illustrative example, with numbers chosen only to show the arithmetic and not as measured or target values: if filling pressure is 12 mm Hg and right atrial pressure is 4, the gradient is 8 mm Hg; if a breath raises right atrial pressure to 9 while filling pressure stays at 12, the gradient falls to 3. In a hypovolemic patient whose filling pressure starts at 7, the same rise in right atrial pressure from 4 to 7 closes the gradient entirely. The arithmetic does not give the flow in any real patient, because filling pressure can move with the breath and resistance is not known.

Every positive-pressure breath is also a circulatory event. A positive-pressure breath raises intrathoracic pressure, and with it right atrial pressure. If right atrial pressure rises more than filling pressure over that breath, the gradient narrows, and with venous resistance unchanged, venous return falls. More breaths, or breaths held longer, keep that gradient narrowed for more of each minute. With less blood entering the heart, each compression has less to eject, and coronary perfusion pressure tends to fall. The prediction weakens when filling pressure rises with the breath, and the same rise in right atrial pressure costs a smaller fraction of venous return when filling pressure starts high: a volume-loaded or venoconstricted patient tolerates the same breath better, while a hypovolemic patient loses venous return sooner. In a study of 10 anesthetized adults undergoing defibrillator implantation, holding airway pressure at 15 rather than 0 cmH2O during apnea raised right atrial pressure and mean systemic filling pressure (measured during brief induced VF) by similar amounts, so the gradient was unchanged, yet left ventricular stroke volume fell by a mean of 23% (with wide variation); that is one bounded observation, not a description of the arrested circulation during CPR. The guideline names the harms of excessive ventilation directly: gastric inflation, regurgitation, aspiration, and decreased cardiac output.

During CPR this reasoning applies with two differences. The heart is not lowering right atrial pressure by ejecting, so the release phase of each compression, when the chest recoils and intrathoracic pressure falls, is the main opportunity for the right atrial pressure to drop below filling pressure and for blood to return. And the same right atrial pressure now sits downstream of two gradients at once: the venous return that refills the heart and the coronary perfusion that nourishes it. A rise in intrathoracic pressure that raises right atrial pressure therefore tends to narrow both. This is physiological reasoning built from the relations above; mean systemic filling pressure is not measured during clinical resuscitation, and the recommendation to avoid excessive ventilation rests on the guideline's statement of harms and on animal and observational data rather than on trials that titrated ventilation to a venous-return target.

The airway state determines the rhythm of breathing. Without an advanced airway the ratio is 30 compressions to 2 breaths. With an advanced airway in place, give 1 breath every 6 seconds (10 breaths per minute) without pausing compressions. Begin with a bag-mask and oxygen. If placing an advanced airway would interrupt compressions, defer it until initial CPR and defibrillation have failed, or until there is ROSC.

questions.prompt: Predict: the patient is intubated and the bag is being squeezed every 2 or 3 seconds to give more oxygen. What will that do to the circulation, and what rate should replace it?
questions.answer: It is roughly 20 to 30 breaths per minute, and it is likely to reduce venous return and the perfusion that compressions create, as well as risking gastric inflation, regurgitation, and aspiration. With an advanced airway, the rate is 1 breath every 6 seconds, enough to see the chest rise.
questions.causalChain: Each breath raises intrathoracic pressure. More breaths per minute keep it raised for more of the time, which tends to reduce venous return. With less blood in the heart, each compression ejects less, and coronary perfusion pressure tends to fall. The guideline names the result as decreased cardiac output.
questions.assumption: Blood oxygen is not limited by ventilation at the slower rate. During CPR, blood flow is low, so 10 breaths per minute at an adequate tidal volume is usually enough to match it.
questions.misconception: The belief that more breaths mean more oxygen delivered. Oxygen delivery depends on blood flow as well as oxygen content, and overventilation lowers the flow. Continued after ROSC, the same excess also lowers PaCO2 and constricts cerebral arterioles.

principles.title: Peri-intubation deterioration and gas trapping
body: Intubation changes three things at once, and each can push a fragile circulation into arrest. Induction drugs remove sympathetic tone, lowering mean systemic filling pressure. Positive-pressure ventilation raises intrathoracic and right atrial pressure. And the transition can remove a patient's own respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis if the ventilator delivers less minute ventilation than the patient was generating. A patient who was already short of volume or acidemic before the tube has the least reserve.

Gas trapping adds a fourth mechanism. When expiration is too short for the lungs to empty, as in severe asthma and, by the same physiology, in COPD or rapid bagging, each breath starts before the last has left. Volume and pressure accumulate in the alveoli (intrinsic PEEP, or auto-PEEP), intrathoracic pressure rises, right atrial pressure rises, and venous return falls by the same mechanism as a tension pneumothorax, but on both sides. The prediction is falling blood pressure, then PEA, with high airway pressures and quiet but equal breath sounds. Brief disconnection from the bag or ventilator lets the chest empty and may relieve hyperinflation; a rise in pressure soon after is consistent with gas trapping. The graded scope is therapeutic and limited to life-threatening asthma refractory to standard therapies, where active exhalation maneuvers may be considered (COR 2b, LOE C-EO); extending it to COPD or rapid bagging is physiological reasoning, not a graded recommendation. A sudden rise in peak pressure or difficulty ventilating in severe asthma should prompt evaluation for tension pneumothorax, which disconnection does not relieve. In life-threatening asthma, a low respiratory rate and tidal volume is reasonable (COR 2a, LOE C-LD).

What remains uncertain: in the arrested patient, the relative weight of these mechanisms usually cannot be measured, and more than one is often present. The timing, arrest within minutes of the tube, is the strongest clue that the procedure changed the physiology.

questions.prompt: Transfer: a hypotensive septic patient is intubated after induction and arrests within three minutes. The rhythm is a fast, narrow PEA and the capnography waveform is present. Using the filling and obstruction categories, which causes compete, and what would distinguish them?
questions.answer: Three causes compete. Induction drugs remove sympathetic tone and positive pressure raises right atrial pressure, so a patient short of volume loses venous return; a tension pneumothorax from positive pressure obstructs it; and a severe metabolic acidosis loses its respiratory compensation if the ventilator rate is lower than the patient's own. A present waveform makes esophageal intubation less likely. Unilateral signs and rising airway pressure point to tension, a pre-intubation blood gas and breathing pattern point to acidosis, and the shock state before induction points to filling.
questions.causalChain: Before intubation, venous return was sustained by vasoconstriction keeping mean systemic filling pressure up and by negative-pressure breathing keeping right atrial pressure low. Venous return is approximately mean systemic filling pressure minus right atrial pressure, divided by the resistance to venous return. Induction lowers filling pressure, and positive pressure raises right atrial pressure. The gradient narrows whenever right atrial pressure rises more than filling pressure; venous resistance does not change the gradient, but a higher resistance lowers the flow a given gradient produces. In a study of 10 anesthetized adults (Jellinek 2000), positive airway pressure during apnea raised both pressures by similar amounts, leaving their difference unchanged, yet stroke volume fell, so the gradient alone did not predict the fall; a higher resistance to venous return or effects on the ventricles must account for it. An underfilled patient has less room for filling pressure to rise, so output can fall below the threshold for a pulse.
questions.assumption: The tube is in the trachea, which the waveform supports but does not prove if pulmonary blood flow is very low.
questions.misconception: The belief that an arrest right after intubation is a coincidence or a drug reaction alone. Its timing is the clue that the procedure changed the physiology.

principles.title: Reading the resuscitation
explanation: End-tidal CO2 links ventilation back to circulation. When an endotracheal tube is used, continuous waveform capnography plus clinical assessment is the most reliable confirmation that it is in the trachea. During CPR, carbon dioxide reaches the lungs only as fast as blood carries it there, so end-tidal CO2 tracks pulmonary blood flow. But it has many determinants: the rate and volume of ventilation, tube position, metabolic production, and drugs such as epinephrine. A change in the number is a prompt to ask which of those changed.

The path the CO2 takes explains why. Carbon dioxide is made in the tissues, as the end product of aerobic metabolism in the mitochondria, and it diffuses from the cells into the capillary blood. Venous blood carries it mostly as bicarbonate, with smaller amounts dissolved in plasma and bound to hemoglobin, back through the right heart and the pulmonary arteries to the pulmonary capillaries. There it diffuses into the alveoli and is breathed out. The capnograph samples the exhaled gas, and the end-tidal value is the partial pressure of CO2, in mm Hg, at the end of exhalation, when the gas leaving the tube comes mostly from the alveoli. It is a partial pressure in gas, not an amount of CO2, not a blood pressure, and not a flow, although during CPR it moves with flow.

Arterial and end-tidal CO2 are related but not the same. PaCO2 is the partial pressure of CO2 in arterial blood; end-tidal CO2 is its partial pressure in exhaled gas. They are close only when the ventilated alveoli are also well perfused. Alveoli that receive gas but little blood, alveolar dead space, add gas with almost no CO2 to the exhaled mixture and dilute it, so end-tidal CO2 falls below PaCO2 and the gap between them widens. During CPR, pulmonary blood flow is low and probably unevenly distributed, so much of the ventilated lung is likely to behave this way, and end-tidal CO2 cannot be read as a stand-in for PaCO2.

That dependence is what makes the number useful during CPR. If metabolic production and ventilation are roughly steady, the main limit on how much CO2 reaches the alveoli is how much blood passes through the lungs, which is the output the compressions are generating. End-tidal CO2 then behaves as a proxy for cardiac output, and its trend is more informative than any single value. Several other inputs move it, and each acts at a different point on the path. Faster or larger breaths wash CO2 out of the alveoli and lower the reading without any change in flow. Sodium bicarbonate generates CO2 as it buffers acid, so the reading can rise after a dose without any improvement in flow. Epinephrine is among the factors the guideline lists; in a human study, end-tidal CO2 fell by a variable amount after a dose, so a fall soon after epinephrine need not mean weaker compressions. A dislodged, kinked, or obstructed tube removes or distorts the gas the capnograph is sampling. And anything that suddenly blocks blood from reaching the lung, such as a tension pneumothorax or a large embolus, lowers the reading by the same route as weak compressions.

A bedside example shows how these compete. With the tube secure and ventilation unchanged, a steady fall over a minute or two after a compressor has been working for a long time points first to fatigue and falling depth. The same fall right after the team speeds up the bag rate points first to washout. The number is identical; the history of what changed is what separates the two. The 2025 guideline notes that values above 10 mm Hg, and ideally above 20 mm Hg, are associated with higher rates of ROSC and may indicate mechanically adequate compressions; that rests on association with ROSC, not on trials of titrating CPR to a value.

Because the number has so many inputs, it is better used as a question than as a verdict. A low or falling value asks first whether the compressions have weakened or the tube has moved, and only later whether the patient can be resuscitated. Even then it should not decide the matter alone: in an intubated adult, failure to exceed 10 mm Hg after 20 minutes of ALS may be one part of a multimodal decision to stop. A sudden rise can accompany ROSC, though no single cutoff proves it, so the rise prompts a pulse check rather than replacing one.

questions.prompt: Predict: in PEA with an advanced airway, end-tidal CO2 has held near 25 mm Hg for several minutes with the same ventilation rate. It suddenly drops to 8 mm Hg. Name the competing explanations, and the order in which you test them.
questions.answer: With ventilation unchanged, a sudden fall means less CO2 is reaching the exhaled gas. The quickest explanations to test are a displaced or obstructed tube and a fall in compression quality. If both are excluded, a new obstruction to pulmonary blood flow, such as a tension pneumothorax, becomes more likely.
questions.causalChain: End-tidal CO2 needs blood to carry CO2 to ventilated lung and a patent airway to carry it out. A dislodged tube removes the second; a tired compressor, a change of hands, or a pause reduces the first; a tension pneumothorax or a new embolus blocks blood from reaching the lung. Each of these can produce the same number, so the number tells you to look, not where.
questions.assumption: Ventilation really was constant, and no drug was just given. A recent dose of epinephrine can change the reading by itself, which makes a fall just after a dose weaker evidence of lost flow.
questions.misconception: The belief that a falling end-tidal CO2 is a prognosis. Here it is a signal that something changed, and several of the candidates are quickly correctable.

questions.prompt: Transfer: end-tidal CO2 has fallen from 18 mm Hg to 8 mm Hg, and the team starts discussing whether to stop. What could have changed, and what do you check first?
questions.answer: Check CPR quality and airway position first: rate, depth, recoil, interruptions, and whether the tube is still in the trachea. A falling end-tidal CO2 is a signal about blood flow or ventilation, not a standalone reason to stop.
questions.causalChain: With steady ventilation, end-tidal CO2 during CPR tracks pulmonary blood flow. A fall often means the compressions are moving less blood, often from fatigue, or the airway has moved. A sudden increase in ventilation rate can also lower it by washing CO2 out faster.
questions.assumption: Ventilation has been steady. If the ventilation rate changed, the number partly reflects that, not blood flow.
questions.misconception: Treating the number as a prognosis. The guidelines say end-tidal CO2 is not used in isolation to end a resuscitation. Only in an intubated patient, and only after 20 minutes of ALS, may failure to exceed 10 mm Hg be considered as one element among others.

questions.prompt: Evidence boundary: a minute after epinephrine, end-tidal CO2 falls even though nothing else has changed. Why shouldn't you read that change as a direct measure of better or worse blood flow?
questions.answer: Because epinephrine is among the factors the 2025 guideline lists as affecting end-tidal CO2, so the reading can move after a dose for reasons other than a change in blood flow. A fall after a dose should not, on its own, be read as a loss of flow. The number has several determinants, and a drug can move it in the opposite direction from the quantity you care about.
questions.causalChain: End-tidal CO2 depends on how much CO2 reaches the lungs and how well the ventilated areas of the lung are perfused. Epinephrine raises aortic pressure, which helps coronary perfusion, but the guideline also lists it among the factors that affect end-tidal CO2 and in a prehospital human study the reading fell by a variable amount after a dose. After a dose, the reading can therefore move independently of cardiac perfusion.
questions.assumption: Ventilation and compression quality were truly unchanged across that minute.
questions.misconception: The belief that end-tidal CO2 is a flow meter. It is a surrogate, useful for trends when other variables are stable, and least reliable when several are changing at once.

principles.title: The Hs and Ts are ways the circulation fails
explanation: Not every arrest is a primary electrical failure. When the rhythm is PEA or asystole, the heart is often unable to produce output because something upstream or around it has failed. The 2025 adult algorithm keeps one reversible-cause list: hypovolemia, hypoxia, hydrogen ion (acidosis), hypo- or hyperkalemia, hypothermia, tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, toxins, pulmonary thrombosis, and coronary thrombosis.

The list is easier to use when it is grouped by physiology. Some causes leave the heart with too little to pump: hypovolemia, and the loss of venous return from tension pneumothorax. Some stop the heart from filling or emptying: tamponade and massive pulmonary embolism. Some starve or poison the myocardium itself: hypoxia, coronary thrombosis, acidosis, potassium disturbance, hypothermia, and toxins. Each group predicts what will and won't help.

The first group fails before blood reaches the heart. In hypovolemia the deficit is volume: blood or fluid has left the vessels, the stressed volume that stretches the veins shrinks, and mean systemic filling pressure falls toward right atrial pressure, so the gradient that drives venous return narrows from the upstream end. In tension pneumothorax the volume may be normal, but air trapped in one pleural space raises the pressure around the heart and great veins, and right atrial pressure rises toward filling pressure, so the same gradient narrows from the downstream end. Both leave the ventricles underfilled, and an underfilled ventricle ejects little whatever its rhythm or contractility. The prediction changes with what is added: a patient who is both bleeding and under tension has the gradient attacked from both sides, and treating one leaves it narrowed. During resuscitation the meaning is that compressions can only move the blood that is in the chest, and the treatment is to restore volume or release the trapped air, as the cause entries below describe.

The second group fails at the heart itself, in the space around it or the vessel leaving it. In tamponade, fluid in the pericardium raises the pressure outside the chambers; the right atrial reading is high, but the transmural pressure that distends the chambers is small, so the heart cannot expand to receive blood. In massive pulmonary embolism the obstruction lies downstream of the right ventricle: clot in the pulmonary arteries raises the pressure the right ventricle must eject against, the right ventricle dilates and fails, and little blood crosses the lungs to fill the left heart. The two can look alike at the bedside, with distended neck veins and a fast, narrow PEA, because both raise right atrial pressure while the left ventricle is starved of volume. A high right atrial pressure in either condition also raises the outlet pressure of the coronary bed described in 3.1, so relaxation-phase aortic pressure buys less coronary perfusion. Compressions and vasopressors push against the obstruction rather than removing it, which is why drainage, decompression, or reperfusion of the pulmonary arteries is the treatment that changes the physics.

The third group leaves filling intact and injures the pump or its electrical control. Hypoxia lowers arterial oxygen content, so the same flow delivers less oxygen to the myocardium; coronary thrombosis stops flow to a region of muscle; acidosis, potassium disturbance, hypothermia, and many toxins alter the ion channels, the calcium handling, or the energy supply on which depolarization and contraction depend. Here the distinction drawn in 4.1 matters: the heart may still depolarize in an organized way while contracting weakly, or it may be driven into VF. A rhythm can suggest one of these causes, but it does not diagnose it, because the same rhythm arises from several and one cause can produce several rhythms over time. What changes the prediction is duration and combination, and a heart that has been ischemic or acidotic for longer is likely to respond less to correction. During resuscitation, the treatment is specific to the cause: oxygen and ventilation for hypoxia, correction of potassium, rewarming, an antidote or targeted drug for a toxin, and reperfusion for coronary occlusion.

This is why compressions and epinephrine alone often fail in these arrests. Compressions do little to fill an empty ventricle, and they do not drain a tamponade, decompress a tension pneumothorax, or open an occluded coronary artery. Epinephrine raises arterial tone, but it does not remove an obstruction. The cause has to be found and treated while compressions continue. Point-of-care ultrasound can be used by an experienced operator to look for a reversible cause when it does not interrupt CPR, though its usefulness during arrest is not well established.

Calcium and sodium bicarbonate show how a plausible mechanism can outrun the evidence. Undifferentiated arrest means the cause is unknown, not that no cause is present, and four different statements need to be kept apart here. Routine use is not recommended: giving either drug to every arrest, without a specific indication, has not improved survival in randomized and registry evidence, and routine calcium has a signal toward harm. Benefit is uncertain in some specific settings: in arrest suspected to be from hyperkalemia, the benefit of intravenous calcium and of intravenous sodium bicarbonate is not well established. A mechanism being plausible is not the same as it being established in this patient, which usually cannot be confirmed during CPR. And none of this makes either drug contraindicated; it makes them targeted rather than default. Calcium is reasonable for life-threatening calcium-channel blocker poisoning and for arrest in a pregnant patient receiving intravenous magnesium. Sodium bicarbonate should be used for life-threatening tricyclic antidepressant cardiotoxicity, and it is reasonable for life-threatening cardiotoxicity from sodium-channel blockers other than tricyclic and tetracyclic antidepressants. A long resuscitation is not, by itself, a reason to give either drug.

The groups describe mechanisms, not patients, and the causes interact. Hypovolemia worsens the acidosis that follows low flow, acidosis blunts the response to catecholamines, hypoxia and acidosis together depress contractility, and positive-pressure ventilation can turn a marginal venous return into an inadequate one. A patient may carry one cause from each group at once. The practical consequence is to keep looking after the first cause is found and treated, and to judge each intervention by whether the circulation changes rather than by whether the explanation seemed complete. This is reasoning from physiology; the guideline supports searching for and treating reversible causes during CPR, but it does not rank them or show that this grouping improves survival.

The limit of the model: during arrest you often cannot confirm the cause, and several can coexist. The categories help you decide what to look for and what to treat on suspicion, not prove the diagnosis.

questions.prompt: Predict: the monitor shows a slow organized rhythm, there is no pulse, and the patient has had two doses of epinephrine. What would you expect a third dose to change if the cause is a tamponade?
questions.answer: Very little. Epinephrine can raise coronary perfusion pressure during compressions, but it cannot relieve a tamponade. While the tamponade persists, the organized rhythm is unlikely to produce a pulse; relieving it is what gives the rhythm a chance to.
questions.causalChain: In tamponade, pressure in the pericardium stops the heart from filling. Without filling there is little stroke volume, whatever the rhythm or the vascular tone. Removing the pericardial fluid restores filling, and then the organized electrical activity can produce output.
questions.assumption: Tamponade is actually the cause. The same reasoning applies to hypovolemia, tension pneumothorax, and massive pulmonary embolism, each of which needs its own treatment.
questions.misconception: The belief that repeating the drug is the plan. Epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes and the search for a cause happen together; neither replaces the other.

questions.prompt: Transfer: someone asks for calcium and sodium bicarbonate because the arrest has gone on a long time. Using the physiology, what is the default answer, and what would change it?
questions.answer: Do not give either drug just because time has passed. Routine calcium and routine bicarbonate are not recommended, and in arrest suspected from hyperkalemia their benefit is not well established. Specific causes change the answer: calcium for life-threatening calcium-channel blocker poisoning or arrest in a pregnant patient on intravenous magnesium, and bicarbonate for tricyclic or other sodium-channel blocker toxicity.
questions.causalChain: These drugs treat specific mechanisms, such as calcium-channel blockade or sodium-channel blockade. In undifferentiated arrest the cause is unknown, so the mechanism the drug targets has not been established in this patient. Given routinely across such arrests, trials and registry data have not shown better survival, and routine calcium leans toward harm.
questions.assumption: The duration of the resuscitation tells you nothing about which mechanism is present. A long resuscitation is a reason to recheck CPR quality and the H and T list.
questions.misconception: The belief that a drug which makes physiological sense must help. Hyperkalemia is the clearest example, where the mechanism is plausible but the benefit during arrest is not well established.

questions.prompt: Evidence boundary: why is it useful to sort the Hs and Ts by physiology rather than memorize the list, and what can't that sorting tell you?
questions.answer: Grouping the causes by what fails tells you what kind of treatment each one needs and why compressions alone won't fix it. It cannot tell you which cause is present in this patient.
questions.causalChain: Causes that empty the heart need volume or decompression, causes that obstruct it need the obstruction removed, and causes that injure the myocardium need the injury reversed. That links each cause to an action.
questions.assumption: One cause dominates. Arrests often have more than one, and you usually can't confirm them during CPR, so some treatment happens on suspicion.
questions.misconception: The belief that a framework is a diagnosis. The grouping guides the search; history, examination, and ultrasound when it doesn't interrupt CPR narrow it.
